extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students learning proof techniques (sets, logic, cardinality, elementary number theory)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and worked solutions for writing correct elementary mathematical proofs (direct, contradiction, bijections, divisibility, countability). Emphasizes common pitfalls, construction techniques, and explicit verification (injective/surjective, cases, inverses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin proofs from hypotheses (avoid backwards write-up)
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing a formal proof, start from the hypothesis and derive the conclusion rather than beginning with the conclusion and working backward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scratchwork may proceed by working backwards from the desired result, but the formal write-up should start with the hypothesis. Anti-pattern: starting with the conclusion and ending with the hypothesis (backwards proof).

rubrics_metrics.name: Define variables and assumptions explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: Before using symbols (a, b, k, ℓ, x, n, etc.) state what they are (integers, natural numbers, real numbers) and any assumptions (e.g., a, b odd; n even).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text criticizes proofs that introduce variables 'out of nowhere' and shows corrected rewrites that begin 'Let a and b be odd integers...' to avoid ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never divide by a quantity that may be zero
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid dividing both sides of an equation by an expression that could be zero under the assumptions (e.g., dividing by x−y when x=y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example anti-pattern: assuming x=y then dividing by (x−y) leads to dividing by zero. Always check denominators or justify nonzero before dividing.

rubrics_metrics.name: When proving bijectivity, use injective+surjective or inverses
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a function is bijective, either prove it is injective and surjective, or exhibit both a left and a right inverse (or the explicit inverse).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text examples: show injective+surjective or show function has both a left and a right inverse; when inverse known (e.g., log) use it to prove bijectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct explicit bijections for cardinality arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: When showing two sets have the same cardinality, give an explicit bijection (e.g., g(q)=π+q, g(q)=πq, h(x)=log(−x−29) after appropriate domain shifts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book emphasizes constructing explicit maps rather than informal 'shifting' intuition; check injectivity and surjectivity or give inverses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use diagonalisation and enumerations for denumerability
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove countability of product sets or unions of countable sets, use diagonal (Cantor-style) enumerations or sweep over diagonals in an infinite table.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: proving N×N is denumerable via diagonalisation; listing elements of each An in rows and sweeping diagonals to enumerate union.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle decimal-expansion constructions with care (avoid ambiguity)
rubrics_metrics.description: When interleaving decimal expansions (e.g., mapping (a,b) → 0.a1b1a2b2...), take care with non-unique expansions (0.4999... = 0.5000...) to ensure injectivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text warns 'Some care is required to ensure that this mapping is injective' and implies resolving ambiguous expansions is necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: When constructing piecewise bijections, ensure surjectivity and continuity as required
rubrics_metrics.description: Piecewise-defined maps intended to be bijections must be checked for jumps or omitted values; correct constructions adjust constants to cover full codomain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: attempted h(x) using 1/x and 1/(x−1) jumped from 2 to −2; fixed by adding ±2 on pieces to restore surjectivity; must then prove bijection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove countability of shifted/scaled rational-derived sets by explicit mapping
rubrics_metrics.description: Sets formed by shifting or scaling rationals (e.g., {π+q}, {πq}) are denumerable because explicit bijections to Q (q↦π+q or q↦πq) can be given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text advises to define the bijection and check it works; also generalize from special case (a=π) to arbitrary a by verifying the same argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Cantor–Schröder–Bernstein via injections both ways
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove two sets are equinumerous, it suffices to give injections A→B and B→A and invoke Cantor–Schröder–Bernstein.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: show |(0,1)| = |(0,1)^2| by an easy injection (x↦(x,1/2)) and a more careful injection back using interleaving decimals; cite the theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: When proving results about unions, work with disjoint partitions
rubrics_metrics.description: For unions of countable sets that may overlap, define disjoint sets Bn by removing earlier elements (Bn = An  igcup_{i< n}Ai) and apply countability arguments to the disjoint union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text gives explicit construction B1=A1, B2=A2\,A1, etc., and shows union of Bn equals union of An and enables applying results for disjoint unions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reusing the same symbol for unrelated integers
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not reuse variables (like k) to denote different integer multiples in different parts of a proof; introduce distinct symbols for distinct multiples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example faulty proof reused k for both a|b and b|c leading to incorrect inference c=k^2 a; corrected write-up uses distinct k, ℓ and composes them.

rubrics_metrics.name: When manipulating inequalities, track sign changes when dividing
rubrics_metrics.description: If you multiply or divide an inequality by a negative quantity, you must flip the inequality sign; be careful when denominators may be negative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: errors arose when dividing by 3x−5 (negative when x<0) without flipping sign; formal proofs should handle cases or justify the sign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove divisibility statements by expressing integers as multiples and algebraic manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: To show n divides an expression, write involved integers as multiples (a = nk, b = nℓ) and manipulate algebraically to factor out n and exhibit an integer multiplier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text shows several divisibility proofs (e.g., if 2|a and 3|a then 6|a) by explicit substitution and factoring to obtain n(times integer).

rubrics_metrics.name: For biconditionals, prove both directions explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving statements like 'n = ⌊x⌋ iff x is integer', show both implications separately (assume n=x ⇒ x integer; assume x integer ⇒ x=n) with justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text demonstrates proving each implication and notes biconditional equivalence arises from combining them; follow same pattern for other iff statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate proof style for the claim (cases, contrapositive, contradiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose the proof method that fits: direct proof, proof by contradiction, contrapositive, or case analysis for piecewise or sign-dependent statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: proof by contradiction used to show impossibility (a^2+b^2=0 with a,b>0), contrapositive used for parity/divisibility statements, cases used for finite vs infinite unions.

rubrics_metrics.name: When presenting solutions, justify each algebraic step and name the rule used
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid terse leaps; show why each step follows (factoring, rearrangement, substitution) so logical errors (like dividing by zero) are evident and avoidable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text rewrites terse student solutions to include intermediate explanations, e.g., list of steps showing where division by zero occurs, or why a sum belongs to Z.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mind notation and typographical conventions in written mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Use conventional symbols (∈, N, Z) and math mode when typesetting; use lowercase for elements and uppercase for sets as standard to avoid confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book criticizes sloppy mixing of text and math (using 'in' instead of ∈, not italicizing math in LaTeX) and recommends conventional, clear notation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle special/edge cases explicitly (e.g., empty sets, zero, ambiguous expansions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't assume intuitive behavior holds in boundary cases: check empty set vs {0} vs {∅}; check behavior when functions blow up or when decimal expansions are non-unique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: empty set vs {0} distinction; checking behavior at x=y in algebraic manipulations; handling 0.4999... vs 0.5000... in decimal interleaving maps.
